utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. We understand there is a matter that you wish to raise, Mr. Rodic, is it, or Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Yes, there is indeed something that we believe should be discussed before we start today's hearing. Yesterday, we received a report from a psychiatrist appointed by the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia to carry out psychiatric examination of Dr. Pavle Strugar on behalf of the Defence team. Yesterday afternoon, although it was not a working day, we filed this report with the CV of the doctor attached. We have also attached a brief document drafted by the Defence team. We tried to inform the Chamber's assistant. We failed, however, but we did manage to get in touch with our learned friends and colleagues from the Prosecution. And we did tell them about this, so they have been informed that this would be our first issue today. I am not sure if the report I am talking about has reached you officially. If it hasn't, it will be forwarded to you in the course of the day. You do, however, Your Honour, remember, I am certain, that the Defence has on a number of different occasions required a psychiatric examination to be carried out. We filed a request like that at the time the trial was first scheduled. We filed a motion in writing in late November. I believe it was on the 27th of November. We raised this issue at the Pre-Trial Conference, as you will remember. We drafted a motion and required a 74 bis Rule, medical examination, which you ruled upon on the 19th of December last year. Your decision rejected our motion for a psychiatric examination of the accused to be conducted, but a possibility was left open for the Defence following agreement with the Trial Chamber and in compliance with the Rules of this Tribunal to organise a medical examination -- such medical examination as is deemed necessary. On the 11th of January this year, the Registry passed their decision accepting the Defence's motion and proposal and appointed Dr. Dusanka Lecic as the psychiatrist that would prepare an expert opinion on the psychiatric state and condition of the accused, Pavle Strugar. We received this report yesterday. The essence of the report is as follows, prior to which I would like to point out that this is a very detailed, in-depth report made on the basis of two sessions that Dr. Lecic had with the accused Pavle Strugar at the Detention Unit. All the necessary tests were conducted during these two sessions. So on these occasions, all the necessary tests were carried out that are prescribed by the World International Organisation and the International Association of Psychiatrists because these are the two references that we have here. Dr. Lecic conducted these tests, examinations, and the results are known to you today, Your Honours. You have them, or should have them in front of you. The essence of the diagnosis established by Dr. Lecic is that Mr. Pavle Strugar has displayed signs of the following illnesses of a psychiatric nature: There are three conclusions, vascular dementia being the first one, the second one being depression, and the third one being PTSD, post traumatic stress disorder. Dr. Lecic also took into account in her report the Somatic illnesses that the accused Pavle Strugar is suffering from. The overall conclusion based on the examinations she conducted is that there are serious cognitive deficits in such areas as are of essence for the proper functioning of the accused. He is, namely, unable to memorise new content or to remember old things. He is unable to establish the necessary level of concentration to follow the trial. There is the problem of the short attention span, and the report lists several other problems which I hope you will receive as soon as possible. The Defence has initiated the need for these medical examinations because ever since we first started representing Mr. Strugar, the level of cooperation of Mr. Strugar in terms of preparing his Defence has been worrying low. The communication between us, the Defence team on the one hand, and the accused is very basic and rudimentary, and it never goes as far as the very essence of the case that is being tried before this Tribunal, where Mr. Strugar stands accused. This was the initial important signal which led the Defence to believe that the issue of Pavle Strugar's ability to actively follow and take part in the trial should be brought up. Based on these three diagnoses established by Dr. Lecic and based on the influence of illnesses that are present in Mr. Strugar's case, these illnesses being directly connected with his psychiatric condition, Dr. Lecic reached the conclusion that the accused, Pavle Strugar, is not able to follow the proceedings and is not healthy enough to be tried before this Tribunal. I also wish to inform the Trial Chamber that this is a very experienced medical expert who teaches at the faculty of medicine in Belgrade and is a member of numerous international health organisations and doctors' organisations, a doctor who has worked on numerous projects related to the area. On the discussion, the Defence team believe that this is a well-founded expert report, expert medical report, which deserves to be taken into serious consideration. We also believe it is important to point out the following: This is the first report of this kind, the first comprehensive report related to the psychiatric condition of the accused, Pavle Strugar. You will remember that at the Pre-Trial Conference, numerous medical documents were put forward that were not as comprehensive, but only referred to individual psychiatric and physical problems which Mr. Pavle Strugar displayed at the time. This report is of a more comprehensive nature. It is a very detailed, in-depth report, very specific, and the conclusion of this report is completely unambiguous and crystal clear. The conclusion drawn by Dr. Lecic is that at this point in time Dr. Strugar is simply unable to proceed because his state of health is not sufficiently good for that to enable him to closely follow the proceedings and actively take part in the trial. I would like to use this opportunity to remind the Trial Chamber that all we've had so far was a report by a general practitioner obtained on the 16th of December last year by the Detention Unit doctor on duty. You remember that this was a medical report drafted by a GP which contains a single sentence. No detailed analysis whatsoever was included. This report stated that all the conditions were in place to commence the trial. There is another important thing that I wish to point out. This report has now been drafted. All the medical expertise available so far has been used and taken into consideration in the drafting of this report from Dr. -- From General Strugar's unfortunately long medical history. As far as this new report is concerned, I would merely like to point out the continuity that exists between Dr. Kmetic's report dated the 25th of November 2001. I'm referring to this expert opinion, although I do not believe that this report is any more detailed, comprehensive, or more relevant than the remaining reports which have been made in the meantime. However, this was a report made by an independent expert appointed by the Registry of the ICTY in November 2001. The original situation was the same or similar to the one we are facing today. Having reviewed this report, the Defence believes that since the time the report was made, Pavle Strugar has not regained a sufficiently good health condition to be able to follow proceedings before this Tribunal. We believe that any further proceedings would seriously jeopardise his rights as an accused before this Tribunal. He does not have the necessary presence of mind to follow proceedings, and therefore cannot be tried. The Defence wishes to reiterate its openness and emphasise that we would welcome any revision of Dr. Lecic's findings as ordered by the Trial Chamber, should the Trial Chamber wish to order any further examinations and reports. As I have already said, our contact with Mr. Strugar has been very difficult, and we have hardly been able to receive any assistance from him Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in preparing this case. As laymen in the science of psychiatry, we were under a certain impression which has since been confirmed by an expert. We would like to ask two things of the Trial Chamber: Firstly, this trial has entered Day 19, and it should be stopped. We would ask of the Trial Chamber to take any decision that the Trial Chamber deems necessary to verify this expert opinion, if it should be deemed necessary. We don't believe it is necessary, but should the Trial Chamber decide that it is, verification should be carried out of Dr. Lecic's expert opinion. Our recommendation is that the trial be stopped. It is in the best interest of justice, and this is in compliance with the sort of jurisprudence that is applied in most legal systems in the world because the accused is simply not able to follow the proceedings due to his health condition. We believe that the report has proved this state of facts efficiently, and this, for us, is sufficient foundation, and sufficient basis, for our request. If, which we don't believe will be the case, the Trial Chamber should rule that in addition to the existence of this comprehensive expert report by an appointed psychiatrist to the effect that the accused Pavle Strugar is not healthy enough to closely follow the proceedings and take part in this trial, and should the Trial Chamber wish to discontinue proceedings immediately after today's hearing, if this is not the case, the Defence would like to file a complaint in which case the Defence would ask for the proceedings to be discontinued until such a motion is ruled on by the Appeals Chamber. We believe this would only amount to fair treatment, and any other course of action, we believe, would severely prejudice Mr. Strugar's rights according to the Statute of this International Tribunal. Thank you very much for your attention, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Petrovic. Could I indicate that we, as a Chamber, have not yet received the report. We were late coming in to Court because one copy of it was handed to us as we waited outside. And we took the opportunity to read through it then quickly. But that is the extent of our familiarity with the report at the present time. Ms. Somers, do you have any submission?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. Thank you, it is true that Mr. Petrovic called me between I would say -- well, sometime around 7-ish, if I'm correct last night, to mention that he was going to be raising this issue. I will say that the accused has been out on provisional release since either late 2001 or early 2002, that there has been ample opportunity if in fact this issue were a bona fide issue, to have been raised and dealt with at that time. As a matter of fact, I am looking to see if the record reflects a 65 ter conference conducted by then legal officer -- senior legal officer Olivier Fourmy of Chamber I where a representation was made because of some insinuations that maybe there would be going down the road of health, that competency would not be raised. Accordingly this issue is not raised for the first time upon Mr. Strugar's having been ordered to return to this Tribunal following a lengthy provisional release, but rather this was raised early on and simply tabled, it appears, until a convenient moment such as introduction of evidence which may or may not be terribly favourable to the accused. The Prosecution suggests that the Defence's assertion that this is proof of condition is wrong. It is one person's opinion. As such, if the Chamber is minded to take action on this, we would certainly hope that a full range of opinions from perhaps more neutral parties may be invoked, and I will again -- now that I have the report, I will speak to my Office and get its position as to whether or not it might seek any of its own independent. However, the Chamber is not advantaged in having been here from the beginning on the dealings on this issue, which in no way is new, and in no way was corroborated by the very lengthy medical reports that came in earlier. This is a person who is aging, and in the normal course of aging certain changes take place. Aggravated, perhaps, as I recall, and again I can only pull it off the top of my head, by other physical maladies. But the timing, I suggest, is the timing of strategy as opposed to the timing of reality. I would ask that if the Chamber is minded to take any action, that it be done contemporaneously with. I can only say the Prosecution, having been -- as the Defence, ordered to move forward is moving forward. Again, with two -- two years plus in provisional release, I find it enormously surprising that in the middle -- 19 days into the trial, we are confronted with this. And I do not trace it back to the December 19th finding of this Chamber. This Chamber, in my view, was not put in a position to make that -- this has a history that predates this panel's arrival. Accordingly, I am not in a position to make positive suggestions now because I also must consider, but I see effectively no evidence that for purposes of today or for purposes of - until further, if any are ordered - examinations there cannot be a continuation of the trial. I take as a great professional affront what I perceive to be an extortionate. We will file a complaint. There are certainly rules that apply, and the Defence is free to do what it will, but it certainly will not hold the Prosecution to that type of extortionate comment. And I cannot speak for how the Chamber receives it. But I am very concerned about timing given the entire history, and I will endeavour, if I can find the discussions from earlier 65 ter conferences. If there's anything further -- again, there are matters which arose in the course of a visit to Montenegro at one point about the General's ability to actively try to assist his own Defence, and should these matters have to be brought to bear, the Office of the Prosecutor will endeavour to have the parties who were privy to that do so. I would, of course, want to see more about the testing. That would go more into if other tests are ordered. But I note there is only a psychiatrist's report, there is no psychologist, and I think this is a fairly early-on piece of information. And again, how the Chamber wishes from here to proceed, I cannot address, but I will say these concerns, I believe, are extremely real on the part of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you just make something a little more clear for me, at least, Ms. Somers. Is it that the Prosecution will be seeking to pursue its own medical examination, or is it that the Prosecution will consider whether it will seek to take that course?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would have to ask for a brief break and speak with my Office, who has not also had a chance -- to not just peruse, but study the report. This is not something that we would -- as I'm sure it was difficult for Your Honours in the hallway to have a review of this. This is not something that one reads lightly. I would ask for an opportunity to discuss it, and I believe it is right for the Chamber also to seek its reports, and of course, if need be, have a full-blown competency hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there anything further, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, not at this point. Our request remains. We believe that the Trial Chamber should urgently rule on this matter. And the other thing I wish to point out is that our medical expert can appear before this Court and testify whenever the Trial Chamber deems necessary as to all the individual aspects of this expert report. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We propose to adjourn temporarily. It may be five minutes, ten minutes, to give some consideration to the submissions that we have had. --- Break taken at 9.36 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber has received this morning a report of a medical expert, Dr. Lecic, which is dated yesterday and which we believe is being filed in the course of this morning. This report is of an examination principally of the mental condition of the accused, Pavle Strugar. And in the report, conclusions are expressed which indicate that in the opinion of the doctor, the accused man is not able adequately to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. follow the proceedings and to instruct counsel. This report raises, of course, issues of considerable significance to the future conduct of this trial; indeed, the future conduct of any proceedings concerning the accused. The Chamber has had only limited opportunity to study the report. It is not the only medical evidence that the Chamber has received. At an early stage of the trial, the previous medical history and reports relating to it of the accused were placed before the Chamber, and we have, over some time, been able to examine them; and indeed, we gave a ruling in respect of them on the 19th of December last year. What is now before us clearly raises new issues and is an expression of opinion which, if well founded and accepted, would indicate that the trial may not be able to proceed, at least at the present time. Because the report is only now in the process of being filed and has not been able to be considered in depth by either the Chamber or the Prosecution, it is our view that we should not immediately come to any view upon it. Indeed, we would expect that when the Prosecution has had an opportunity to consider the report, the Prosecution may well wish itself to advance much more detailed submissions than has been possible this morning, and we would expect that the Prosecution will itself give consideration to the question whether it should pursue its own medical examination of the accused. The Chamber, too, once it has heard the Prosecution's position on that, will need to give consideration to the issue whether it should itself order a medical examination of the accused man. In addition to this report, as I've indicated, the Chamber has had and has studied the detailed material that was provided by the Defence as to the previous medical history of the accused man. What is in this report is not something quite novel; it clearly has its foundations in much that was in the earlier reports. And they date back two and more years, and it is, therefore, of concern to the Chamber that this matter should now be raised in this way when there clearly was notice of the possibility and very, very adequate time for it to have been pursued by the Defence before this trial commenced. While that does not mean that we should ignore the report now, and it certainly will not be ignored, it is a fact relevant to our consideration of how we should deal immediately with the report and its consequences for the conduct of the hearing. We also take into account our previous knowledge from the detailed materials that were placed before us by the Defence, and also the experience the Chamber has had of the past 19 days of the hearing of this trial and the degree to which, when it was appropriate, the accused has participated, including his own personal submissions to the Chamber. In light of all those matters, it is our view that we should not today interrupt the continuation of the hearing. We would propose to continue hearing evidence and to call on the Prosecution to indicate its more studied position either tomorrow morning or the following morning, depending on what Ms. Somers indicates to me would be the time she would need to give consideration to the Prosecution position. Now, we take that course while very mindful of the significance of the possible effects of the report, as Mr. Petrovic has put to us very clearly. But we do say, having regard to the matters I've indicated, in particular, the past medical reports and the apparent condition and degree of participation of the accused in the trial to date, and in particular, we do so on the basis that if it should prove to be the case after there has been an adequate time to consider the report and any other medical reports that prove appropriate, if it should prove to be the case that the accused man is in truth not fit to continue with the hearing, well, then, the trial would have to come to an end and there would be no ultimate injustice; whereas, if at the end of our consideration of all this -- the present and any future material that is placed before us we should reach the conclusion that the trial can properly proceed, we will not have lost time unnecessarily. And as was indicated a little time ago in the course of these brief reasons, the timing and circumstance of the way this issue is raised has been effective. We've taken into account in determining how best to proceed today. For those reasons, therefore, we would propose to continue with evidence today. And until we hear the further submissions of the Prosecution, and we will decide then on what course should be taken. Ms. Somers, are you in a position to indicate today whether you would be ready tomorrow with your more considered position?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, I can, if the Chamber would permit oral submissions, I would be grateful. And I have begun the process, but of course we would need to study it more hopefully this afternoon with my superiors. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, that being the case, then, we'll continue on the basis that I've indicated, Mr. Petrovic, and Mr. Rodic, with the hearing today. And we will hear further submissions on this matter tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. I merely wish to have the following clarification from you: Will you make a final ruling as to whether our motion has been accepted or not tomorrow after you've heard more detailed submissions, or have you already taken a decision? If such a decision has been made, we would like to file an appeal. I would like that clarification, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, we haven't taken a final decision. And it will depend upon the submission that is made tomorrow whether we make a final decision tomorrow. It may well be necessary for time for further medical examination, and it may be necessary for us to then consider the reports, or even to hear the various medical experts before reaching a final decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my apologies, first of all. In my understanding, there are two things that are quite distinct. One is your final ruling concerning the essence of this problem, that is, whether General Strugar is able to follow proceedings and to continue or not. That's what I want to know really, and that's something you've commented on. Secondly, the other thing I want to know about is your decision on our motion to discontinue evidence pending final clarification. That decision, as I understand it, will be taken tomorrow. Am I correct in assuming that, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Our decision today is to continue with evidence today. We will decide tomorrow whether or not we should continue with further evidence or whether an adjournment is necessary. We cannot be confident whether we can make a final decision on even that issue tomorrow, until we've heard the submissions and given more attention to the report that we've received.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, is it convenient to proceed now?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution calls as its next witness Colonel Colm Doyle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel. If you would be able to take the affirmation that will be handed to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, when you're ready.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel Doyle, would you give your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: My name is Colonel Colm Doyle of the Irish defence forces. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And your date of birth, sir.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: The 1st of May 1947.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And can you tell us, please, your current position, and then I will work backward to your military and other background.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: My current appointment is chief of staff of the military division at the department of peacekeeping operations, United Nations headquarters, New York city.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel Doyle, how long have you held that position?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Approximately two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Prior to your assumption of the position, what was your post?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I was a serving colonel in the Irish Defence Forces, and my appointment was director of reserve forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Going a little bit backward from, let's say, 1964, could you run us through, please, your career as a military officer from the time you joined the army up to the most -- the appointment just prior to your becoming chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I became an officer cadet in the Irish Defence Forces in 1964. I was commissioned as second lieutenant in 1966. I was promoted to the rank of captain in 1973. Promoted to the rank of commandant, which is major, in 1979. Promoted to the rank of lieutenant colonel in 1995, and promoted to the rank of Colonel in the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, where or in which territories you may have served over the course of your military career?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I served in a variety of appointments, both command and staff, throughout the various ranks I held in the Irish Defence Forces. In relation to my service abroad, I first served abroad as a member of the United Nations force in Cyprus in 1968 as a platoon commander. In 1978 I served with the 1st Irish unit in service with the United Nations' infantry force in Lebanon. I held the rank of captain. From 1984 to 1986, I was a military observer with the United Nations truce supervision in the Middle East based in Syria, and subsequently in Lebanon where I became the senior operations officer of observer group Lebanon. I've served as a battalion commander with the United Nations forces in Lebanon from 1997 to 1998. And for 12 months commencing on the 1st of October 1991, I served in the former Yugoslavia, initially as a member of the European community monitor mission in the Republic of Bosnia, and thereafter as personal representative to the chairman of the international peace conference, Lord Peter Carrington from April 1992 until I finished at the end of October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel Doyle, did you have a head of mission position for the European community monitor mission during your course in the former Yugoslavia? And if so, what was the area and when were you appointed?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I was in the former Yugoslavia in the Republic of Bosnia for approximately six weeks. And in around the 24th of November, I was asked would I take over the appointment as head of the monitor mission for the Republic of Bosnia based in Sarajevo. And I held that appointment until approximately the end of -- or towards the end of March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you say Bosnia, you're referring to Bosnia and Herzegovina territory?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, before we proceed, can you tell us, please, your formal education, the degrees, if any, that you hold and where they were earned and when, please.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I'm a graduate of the Irish Defence Forces cadet school. I'm a graduate of the Irish Defence Forces infantry school, and I'm a graduate of the Irish Defence Forces command and staff school. I also hold a masters degree in international studies which I attained from the University of Limerick in Ireland in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are there any particular areas in which you may have placed emphasis in the course of your peacekeeping operations?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I suppose I had particular experience in the Middle East, having been there on three occasions. And I would say that when I served in Bosnia, I had a general understanding of the developments which took place in 1991, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you have any background in mediation or negotiation or such skills?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: One of the principles of the United Nations' operations is the ability to be able to mediate and negotiate because particularly when I served in the Middle East from 1984 to 1986, I was an unarmed military observer. Where the officers of the United Nations are used to a great extent by military officers who rely on mediation and negotiation, liaison work, and that's where I had most of my experience. And one of the fundamental principles of service with the United Nations is the degree of impartiality which must be exercised at all times.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. And just one more question ancillary to that: Have you participated yourself or had any direct involvement in cease-fire negotiations throughout any of the service you've had?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I was involved considerably in the former Yugoslavia in cease-fire negotiations, particularly in the city of Sarajevo. I was also instrumental in the hostage negotiations to secure the release of President Ilija Izetbegovic in early May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Let us turn your attention, now, to the autumn of 1991. What were you doing at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Is this prior to service in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: At the time that I was asked would I consider volunteering for Yugoslavia, I was adjutant of the southern Irish brigades' reserve forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Could you explain, please, what adjutant involves?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Adjutant would be a staff appointment held by a military officer that deals with such things as personnel, administration, and discipline.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How did you first become aware of the need for personnel for the ECMM, for the monitoring mission, to the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: The practice in the Irish Defence Forces is that when there is request made by the international community for the availability of military officers, all officers are asked would they be willing to volunteer for service abroad. I would have been one of those. And then the list would have been examined. The Defence forces had called us to ascertain the qualities and the experiences of those officers, and based on the approval of those files they would have made their decision. In that case, I was one of three officers selected for service as a monitor with the European community monitoring mission.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you able to in a very brief manner summarise the qualities that you found yourself to have possessed that would have ensured your having been selected for such a post?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I can only surmise that because I had a successful service in Cypress, in Lebanon, and in the Middle East from 1984 to 1986, it was deemed that I was suitable to serve in another mission area because a lot of what was going to be done we assumed in Yugoslavia was similar to what you would be doing as a military observer with the United Nations, which was basically observing and reporting and getting involved in liaison work and mediation. So I believed I had those attributes which was required for service in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you have any inclination one way or the other to any of the factions or parties involved?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Not specifically. We would have had a general understanding of the general background. We would have received a briefing at Defence Forces headquarters, but it would have been very general in nature and nothing very specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And what was -- did you work to any prescribed mandate?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, the mandate that I worked under when I was in Bosnia was the mandate that was generally prescribed for the monitor mission which was that we were to use our good offices to persuade the parties to desist from any conflict, that any progress to be made was to be made by mediation and negotiation, and if conflict were to break out that we should be there to monitor it in an independent and impartial fashion. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. And also, to attempt to limit the conflict as best we could.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So your -- how would you encapsulate your duty as a monitor? How would you have understood it to be?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: And basically, my duties as a monitor would have been to be deployed to a particular area within the area of operations, which in my case was Bosnia; to make sure that we met with all the parties; that would have included military, religious leaders; to meet with anybody who wished to have conduct with us; to be able to indicate to them what the reason that the monitor mission was there; and also to be able to report back accurately on those aspects of meetings that were deemed to be appropriate and should be reported on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, you had, as I understand it, specific areas of responsibility, regions. And your particular region was head of mission, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes I started off as a member of the monitor mission in a specific area, which was in Banja Luka. But as I said, after about six weeks, I was asked to take over as the regional head of the mission for Sarajevo, which meant that I was covering the entire Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What did you feel appropriate as your first duties to carry out, upon assuming the job, the position of head of mission, for ECMM in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, as head of the mission, I was anxious to ensure that I would make myself available to anybody who wished to contact me. I was also anxious that I would pay a visit to all the areas within Bosnia where we had what we call monitor teams deployed. And also, that I would make myself known to the local leadership and to the senior officers of the JNA Army, and to be able to make myself known to them and what we were about.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you there as a military -- when you made these visits, were you there as a military person, or how did you perceive your role?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I was there as head of the monitor mission. I happened to be military, but I was not there because I was a military person.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were other heads of mission necessarily having military background?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No. The two previous heads of the mission for Bosnia were diplomats from Britain. I was the first military head of the mission for Bosnia. I did not wear a uniform. I was addressed as Mr. Doyle. My own staff addressed me as chief. I was never addressed by my military rank for the period I served there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina is comprised obviously of a number of municipalities. Did you also decide to pay a visit to some of the municipalities bordering other republics?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: At the first municipalities that I visited were the areas up towards Banja Luka. This was the area of my -- what we call the area of operations. When I went to Sarajevo, I deemed that it would be appropriate to visit any of the municipalities where I was asked to visit, and particularly those where we had teams deployed. Some of those were in areas which were dominated by Serbs, some by Croats, and some by Muslim communities. And I felt it was important that we be seen to be impartial by visiting all of the areas and by having our liaison teams deployed to the different areas. And this I set out about to do in the first few weeks of my appointment as head of the mission.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to just confirm, the headquarters where you served as head of mission for ECMM was in which particular city?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: The headquarters were in the Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the course of getting out, on the 6th of December, I want to ask you if you held -- where were you, and if you were was preceded by any meetings before that, if you could please explain to the Chamber what you were doing on behalf of ECMM on that day or just prior.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: This was approximately the second or maybe the third week of my command, and I decided I would visit the teams that we had deployed down in the area of Mostar --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Forgive me, Colonel. 6th December 1991. I apologise for not having given you the time frame.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Early in December I decided that I had -- would make an arrangements to visit the teams that we had deployed in the city of Mostar. So I contacted the team down there to say that I was going to come. I wanted to meet with them. And I also decided that it would be appropriate that I would meet on those visits which I did at various times, the senior JNA military commanders. I was informed by the team that the senior JNA commander in that area was General Strugar, and an arrangement was made for me to meet with him. And that was to be on the 6th of December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And did you, in fact, meet General Strugar in that area on the 6th of December 1991?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I met with General Strugar on the 6th of December, having met with some of the leadership of the city of Mostar earlier that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you know at the time what General Strugar's area of responsibility would have included, what particular geographical points?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I was aware of the fact that the -- that his command area would have included the areas of Trebinje and Bileca. Beyond that, I had no idea how far his command extended.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you know then at the time whether or not his area of responsibility might have included Dubrovnik on the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How did you travel to meet General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I travelled in a car that was allotted to the monitor mission. So I travelled by road from Mostar to Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And was there a particular -- excuse me, Trebinje is in what particular republic?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Trebinje, in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And Mostar also?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you have a -- I call it a working arrangement or a modus operandi for these meetings? Did you have a logistical way of getting to numbers of persons, for example?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: When I would go on a trip of this nature, at my own instigation, I travelled in a car belonging to the monitor mission. I would bring -- I would have a driver, one of my own drivers from the mission, and I would bring with me my senior operations officers and my interpreter. So normally, I would have travelled in a car carrying four people, including myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you have travel alone or on your own?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And why would that have been?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, one of the principles under which we travelled was that we were given a guarantee of freedom of movement and safety and security, and in military terms safety and security would indicate that you should never travel on your own, as well as that if I had meetings with people, I always wanted to have somebody else, a minimum of one other person with me who would be able to verify or who would be there as a witness to who I had met and what I had said. So it made sense to go with somebody else from the mission. This, I always did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Based on what you've just told us, who was travelling with you on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I had an Italian driver. I don't remember his name. I also had my senior operations officer, who was an Irish Army commandant, Dermot Coogan, and I had my interpreter who was with me that day, a man who was allotted to the monitor mission. His name was Darko Ivic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: On the way to the place where the meeting with General Strugar took place, did you hear anything out of the ordinary by any chance?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: On the route from Mostar towards Trebinje, we were aware that we could hear some artillery firing going on. Where it was going to or where it was coming from, I have no idea. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you able to give an approximation of time as to when you met with General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can recollect, and on consulting my diary, I met with General Strugar approximately at 12.00 on the 6th of December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is that toward midday, when you say 12.00?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask, in your statement to the OTP, one of the attachments was a -- an excerpt from the diary.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And I would simply ask at this point to have it passed out, to distribute. It also is up on the screen, Your Honours, on Sanction, to be of help. If I could ask for it, perhaps, to be magnified. I find it a bit difficult to read.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel, looking at a document, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What is it, please?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: It's an entry in my personal diary for Friday, December the 6th, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And what does it say? Perhaps you can decipher your writing.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: 0830 hours, met with the mayor of Mostar. 1200 hours met with General Strugar (three star) and after that I've written "bad in Dubrovnik". And after that I've written back to Mostar, and overnight.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When did you make this entry? I notice it said "met with General Strugar"?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but it was my practice to make -- to fill in the diary the evening or in -- the day after I would have carried out these events.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask to have this exhibit identified and marked for identification and moved into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, did you say you wanted it marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And moved into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Or as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number will be P46.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel, when you got to the location, and if you can give us a rough idea of where it was that you met with the general, what did you find? Were you immediately received? Were you expected?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: The location to the best of my memory was on the outskirts or very close to Trebinje. When I arrived at the location, the general was not immediately available. And I went in with a -- with my operations officers and my interpreter. We were met inside the building by a lieutenant colonel who was interpreting for the general. This lieutenant colonel I had met before when I had met General Kukanjac in Sarajevo. He was the interpreter there as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, who was General Kukanjac?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: General Kukanjac was the senior JNA commander in the city of Sarajevo. I'm sorry

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: So when we went into the general's office, his interpreter informed us that the general was preoccupied. There seemed to have been quite a lot of activity going on. I wasn't sure at that stage whether the general was available to speak with me. And I mentioned to the interpreter that if the general wasn't available, then I would leave. He then asked me if I would stay for another few minutes, and he would ascertain. And about five minutes later he came back to tell me that the general would meet with me. And all together, I think we waited for approximately ten minutes before the general came in to meet us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were any photographs taken at this particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. At the end of the meeting, I asked the general if he would pose for a photograph, and he agreed to do this. And I have a photograph taken which included the general, myself, and my senior operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just ask if I could please -- I believe it will be up on the Sanction screen, but I will also distribute a photocopy, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel Doyle, do you recognise what is in front of you, please?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I recognise it is the photograph that was taken in the company of General Strugar on the 6th of December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask that this be admitted into evidence, please, and I will discuss it a bit later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel Doyle, when you initially met with General Strugar, had you ever met with him before?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, I had not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How did General Strugar appear when he walked into whatever room it was you were to have met with him?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I felt that the general had been preoccupied because of what his interpreter had said to me. And his interpreter had said that he would be made available, but it would be for a relatively short period of time, which was unusual because most of the meetings I had used to go on for quite considerable time. So that was the impression I received at the time, of his demeanour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you observe anything about the general in his demeanour, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Nothing other than getting the impression that he may have been a little bit preoccupied. That was my general feeling.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. Was he -- was there an air of calmness about the general?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, it was the first time I had met the general, so I'm not too -- you know, I'm not too sure whether I would call it that he was calm. But I got -- I did get the impression that he was preoccupied and somewhat restless.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, did this perception of yours persist throughout your later conversation?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, the content of what he said to me led me to believe that he had been preoccupied, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And did you feel he was focussing on the matters you were discussing?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I think he was being courteous to me, but maybe he was focussing on other matters. But I'm not too sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How did you introduce yourself to the general?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I introduced myself by name. I told him who I was representing, what the organisation was, and I told him in general terms what the organisation that I represented was trying to achieve.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How did the meeting progress from that point?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, after I had said this to the general, he spoke some words. And the interpreter informed me that the general had been quite angry because what was termed to me as paramilitaries on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina had attacked some of his troops, the troops that were under General Strugar's command. This was something he would not tolerate and that he responded by firing on the city of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was your reaction to hearing this? What were your initial reactions?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I was taken by surprise at this because I felt it was rather unusual for somebody to make an admission to me that he had taken action against a city.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And what exactly was it that surprised you at his having said that? Why?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I suppose in my 40 years of military experience, it was the first time that anybody had said to me that they had ordered fire to be brought to bear on a city.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What is it about firing on a city that would have perhaps caused some concern to you, or did cause concern to you?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I was concerned because it was my view that firing on a city indicated that there would be civilians there, and there was property there, and that firing on a city was nothing that could be very accurate. And therefore, there might have been casualties or there might have been damage to property. And this actually surprised me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you get any sense of a connection between what you say the general said about firing on Dubrovnik and the issue of paramilitaries? What was your perception of the linkage?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, my perception of the linkage was that the reason why he fired on the city was because paramilitaries on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina had interfered or attacked the troops under his command. And this was his response to that action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: May I intrude, Colonel, to make it clear one matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Was it the -- a member of the general's staff that informed you of this attack and his response? Or was this interpreted as the general spoke it to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To me, this was the interpretation of what the general had said which was spoken to me by the military interpreter. In other words, the interpreter that was acting on behalf of General Strugar. My own interpreter was not involved in this conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Was the general present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was, Your Honour. PROSECUTION COUNSEL:

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Sorry. How long had you been serving as a soldier, if you had to count numerically?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I started to be a soldier in 1964, and this was in 1991. So I would make that I think 27 years, 28 years maybe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In the course of your career as a soldier had you, prior to your meeting with General Strugar and the comment that was made to you by General Strugar, had you ever heard of such a comment being made by a commander?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, I had not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was there any further conversation after that comment was made?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I don't recall in any great detail, but I do know that the meeting maybe lasted for approximately 25 minutes. The interpreter had made it known to me that it would be a relatively short meeting. I accepted this. And I was just grateful that General Strugar had given the time to meet with me. So as far as I can recollect, we left after about 30 minutes, 25 to 30 minutes approximately.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If you could be so kind as to go back to P47, which is the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If you could have that back up, please, or if it's still there, turn your attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If the general had been in the mood in which you described, is there any particular reason why he agreed to have his photo taken?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No. I think it was out of a gesture of courtesy to me because I had asked the general if he would stand in for a photograph because of the significance of the occasion, because I was going around meeting a lot of senior people and I wanted to get a record of this purely for my own diaries. And the general kindly agreed to stand in for the photograph, which took maybe one or two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: On the screen, you can see some writing on the photograph. Do you know whose writing that is? And would it be -- what part of the photograph would that writing be visible from?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I would assume that was on the back of the photograph. It's my writing. I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you read it, please.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, it's dated the 6th -- it's dated the 6th of December 1991. It says: "Left to right, commandant Dermot Coogan senior operations officer, ECMM, General Strugar, OC of the second operations group, and commandant Colm Doyle, chief, ECMM."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: OC, what does that abbreviation stand for, please?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Officer commanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And how did you come to learn of the name "second operational group"?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I wasn't too sure at the start when I had taken some notes on the actual military formations, and it was brought to my notice subsequently that, in fact, the command that General Strugar had was of the 2nd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can I ask you if there are any other comments or any other writing on the photograph, let's say, the backside of it, that we were looking at that you were familiar with?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, on the back of the photograph I had written at that time "with the OC of the 2nd corps group," I had written, "General Strugar on December 6th the day he launched an artillery attack on Dubrovnik killing 16."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You yourself wrote that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have a break now for some 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel Doyle, are you able to give an approximate time when the meeting came to its conclusion.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you repeat that, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Surely. Could you give an approximate time when the meeting came to its conclusion, approximately?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: As best I can recall, approximately 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you record what was said at this meeting anywhere?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, I have no record of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Why would this be? What was special about this type of meeting?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, most of the reports that were made were compiled by the monitor teams that were deployed throughout the republic in various locations. I would give reports that I deemed were appropriate at the time. I suppose on this reason -- on this occasion, the reason I didn't make a report was, number one, I had only just -- this was the first trip I had taken as head of the mission, so I was very new into my assignment. And number two, I was aware that the monitor mission had another mission and operation in Croatia. Its headquarters for that region was in Split. And if any action had been taken against Dubrovnik on that day, I assumed it would have been reported by the mission in Croatia. My mission was specific to the Republic of Bosnia, and I didn't report on anything outside of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Fine. Now, was there any other public coverage of your meeting that day that you made note of or responded to?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. I had a -- there were some people from the presidency of Bosnia who were attached as advisors and assistants to the monitor mission. One of them was the interpreter I made mention of who worked for me, Darko Ivic, and another was a lady called Vera Ljubovic who was also an interpreter on some occasions. I had asked her if she would monitor the local press to be able to give me a translation of articles that appeared that referred to the mission. I felt this would be of benefit. It would give me an idea as to how the mission was being perceived. She came to me a few days after my visit, and she gave me a translation of an extract from the daily paper Oslobodenje, and from the daily paper Borba, and she translated the articles from both of those papers and she gave me a copy of the articles -- I'm sorry, she gave me a copy of the translations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If the usher could be good enough to receive copies of two documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel, both in front of you and on your screen -- you have two documents in front of you, but on your screen you have a document that bears evidence recording number 03340137. Do you recognise that document, or at least the page that's in front of you?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I do. They're the pages of the translation from the daily papers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If I could ask my colleague to perhaps enlarge the portion. If you could, please indicate where it says "Borba, December 9th." If you could read that.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: It refers to a Conan Doyle and some question marks. I presume they got my --- first spelling of my name incorrect. Head of the EC Monitor Mission for BH. And the title of it is To avoid war in Bosnia, and it goes on to say as best I can read, head of the EC monitor -- EC mission, met Lieutenant-General P. Strugar in Trebinje. He noted that the authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina showed respect for the JNA. He is aware of the problem created by the kidnapping of a pilot in Mostar. And the authorities -- I can't read the next three words.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mine looks like --

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: But the authorities assured him, I think, that the problem would be solved as soon as possible or sorted as soon as possible. Strugar stressed that the Croatian paramilitary forces used BH territory for attacks on the JNA which Mr. D. accepted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was there something about this report that concerned you or did you take any action on?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. When I read that translation, I was really annoyed because there was no circumstances under which I accept that Croatian paramilitary forces used BH territory for attacks on the JNA. And I felt that this was either the deliberate or a mistake, because it was General Strugar, my recollection of, who had made that allegation. So accordingly, I made a request through my interpreter that a notification be sent to the paper, and I wished to have a retraction published.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, was such a retraction published --

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, the paper did make a retraction some days later, or a correction some days later.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please to, look at the second document, which is ERN 03340136, and it is on your screens as well, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, this is the article that appeared or a translation that article allegedly that appeared in the paper Oslobodenje December the 8th.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you please help us read it.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: It says head of the monitor mission in Trebinje, Mr. Colm Doyle, and then in brackets, N. B., Mr. -- I don't know if it's the same spelling, Doyle, and what looks like -- I can't really read it. It looks like V62. Head of the BH mission met the official of the 2nd Operational Group of the JNA. In the talks, the commander of the 2nd Op Group, Lieutenant-General Strugar mentioned that Croatian paramilitary forces on the territory of BH to attack army units, stressing that -- it looks like stressing that this was war. Mainly done by the people that are no longer under the control of the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: That's the best translation, or reading that I can make of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'd ask, please, to have these moved into evidence, both documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P48 and P48 A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is that for both, Madam Registrar? There are two documents there.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Is that okay? One number for both documents because I see the English translation on one page only.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: After this meeting, did you ever have occasion to meet personally again with General Strugar; and if so, where?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I didn't have a personal meeting with General Strugar, but I was asked to facilitate a programme of meetings. I -- the Portuguese head of the monitor mission who was based in Zagreb, his name was Ambassador Salgueiro, and he came to visit the mission area in Bosnia in February of 1992. I made a suggested itinerary for that visit, and it included a formal visit to General Strugar's headquarters which I had arranged and which took place. I'm not too sure of the exact date. But Ambassador Salgueiro and all of his officials who came from Bosnia were afforded an opportunity to meet with General Strugar and his officers in his headquarters which I believe at that time were in Bileca. And as head of the monitor mission, I was in attendance for those talks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. At this time, no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Somers. Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in view of the fact that I had a conversation with the general during the break, I must say the general told me that he recognised himself in the photograph, but that he does not know this witness, Mr. Doyle, nor does he remember him. Bearing in mind the initial discussion that we had this morning in connection with the expert finding that has been submitted and what its potential meaning is, the Defence would propose to have the cross-examination of this witness postponed until your ruling tomorrow, the ruling that you have announced on this material issue which was the subject of our first discussion this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that without parsing every aspect of what my learned colleague has just said, the fact of recognition of himself in a photo perhaps has some implications, but that the cross-examination should, in fact, proceed in that the issues are clear, the matters have been presented much earlier on by submissions under the Rules of 66 -- not just A1, but A2, and there has been ample opportunity to prepare this witness for this cross-examination. It has been no secret that this man was going to appear. I see no basis whatsoever for not continuing, and the Chamber's earlier ruling, I believe, covers this and envisages this particular eventuality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, our view is in accordance with our earlier decision and for that reason, you should proceed with your cross-examination now. You clearly have instructions, that the general does not recognise this witness, and you cross-examine on that basis, if necessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I wonder if it would help you if you had the lectern, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just about to ask for the lectern to be given. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Doyle, my name is Goran Rodic. I'm an attorney-at-law, and I will ask you a number of questions on behalf of the accused, General Strugar. Can you please tell me exactly when you arrived in the former Yugoslavia as part of your mission.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I arrived in the former Yugoslavia, to the best of my recollection, on the 1st of October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me where exactly you arrived the first time you came.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I flew from Ireland into Austria, and I went by car from Austria into Zagreb in Croatia, which was the headquarters of the monitor mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how long you were in Zagreb and what you did there.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I was in Zagreb for approximately eight days during which time I received briefings from the headquarters of the mission as to the -- what the mission was about. There was a delay in moving out of Zagreb because there was a cease-fire being negotiated between the head -- the monitor mission, who was Ambassador Dirk van Houten and General Raseta on behalf of the JNA. And thereafter I was initially deployed to Belgrade. I was in Belgrade for approximately two days, and then I was deployed to the city of Sarajevo, which was the headquarters of the monitor mission for the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me about the briefing in Zagreb. More specifically, who was it that briefed you on the situation in the former Yugoslavia at the time? Probably you were also briefed on the problems that the mission would be likely to encounter in its work as well as its tasks. Can you tell us more specifically about the briefing.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I do not recall who gave us the briefing, but most of the monitors who arrived were given general information as to what the mission was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What was the mission about?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: The mission was to attempt to use the influence of the mission to ensure that conflict would be avoided in the republics and that we would attempt to influence that as best we could; and that if conflict were to spread to the republics, that we would do the best we could do contain it. It was inherent in that that we would accurately reflect in an impartial manner the events that were taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I understood what the task of your mission was, but I don't think you answered my question related to the briefing that you had in Zagreb. You don't remember who provided you it, but my assumption is that you were given information on the situation on the ground where you were about to go and work. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I was given no information in relation to the situation on the ground because the decision was not made at that stage as to where I would be working.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you then tell me what you did over those eight days you spent in Zagreb. Were you on some sort of a standby waiting to be sent somewhere, without any information whatsoever as to where you were being sent, or what problems you were likely to face on the ground?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: In essence, yes, that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Had you ever been to the former Yugoslavia before then?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, I had not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the social and political situation and structure of the former Yugoslavia, how the country worked?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Not to any great degree, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you say "not to any great degree," could we perhaps also put it this way: You had very little knowledge of the actual situation?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I believe I had sufficient knowledge to be able to fulfil any function that was given to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Yugoslavia, did you know which was the legal armed force under the then constitution of the former Yugoslavia and under the relevant laws?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I was aware of the fact that the Federal Army, the JNA, was a legal army of the Federation of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you know if there were any other military police or other armed formations present on the ground in the former Yugoslavia? That's in addition to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: For the eight days that I was in Zagreb, I had a general understanding of the overall situation, that there was unrest, for example, in the Republic of Slovenia, that the monitor mission was deployed up there, that an agreement had been made to monitor the withdrawal of the JNA who were going to move out of Slovenia. And the situation both military and political was developing as I was there; therefore, the situation changed quite rapidly. I was aware in general terms of what was going on. But nothing specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: While you were in Zagreb at the headquarters of your mission, was there a siege of JNA army barracks at the time? Was the siege underway? Did the mission based in Zagreb have any tasks related to this developing situation?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: My understanding at that stage was that the EC monitor mission was attempting to facilitate the lifting of the sieges on the various military barracks in that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You said the task of the mission was to use its influence to avoid conflict in the republics. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I would like to correct myself there. I said the task of the mission was to use its influence to avoid the spreading of conflict in the republics. In other words, that the mission wasn't necessarily to avoid conflict, but that the parties were to attempt to avoid conflict between themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What were the republics where this situation was at the time you arrived?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I was aware that there was unrest in the Republic of Slovenia, and that it was gradually moving towards Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Unrest in the Republic of Slovenia, you say. When was that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: That was around the time that I went to former Yugoslavia, and the time before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This is a very general time frame that you've just given us. Can you please try to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it that you don't know, or you don't remember?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: It is more likely that I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me who the parties were. How could conflict arise in Croatia at the time you arrived?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: We were subject to a considerable amount of propaganda when we arrived in Croatia; and therefore, I was not totally au fait with the situation knowing that I was not going to be staying in Croatia, knowing that I was going to be deployed either in Serbia or Bosnia. One of the reasons why I went out to the former Yugoslavia was that there was a decision made within the monitor mission to increase the size of the mission because there was a strong likelihood of the mission deploying down to Bosnia. Therefore, there was a strong likelihood that I would be sent to Bosnia. And therefore, I wasn't totally concerned with the situation in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Would I be right if I said that you were not familiar with the situation in Croatia during the eight days you spent there in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I wasn't to any great detail, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me more about the propaganda that you were subjected to, as you say, during your stay in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: On the ground floor of the hotel, there was an office which was run by the Croatian authorities, and from time to time they would give out periodicals and reports, and these reports would be placed outside the bedrooms of some of the monitors. Certainly outside the bedroom I was in. And I believe inherent in that was an attempt to give a report of the ongoing situation the way that the Croatian authorities would have liked it to have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What was your impression based on, if a moment ago you told us that you were not specifically familiar with the situation in Croatia to any great detail? Why did you have the impression that they were spreading their own view of the developments that they were carrying out, propaganda?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Because I didn't ask for a copy of their material, but it was given to me in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was this the only reason you had that led you to the conclusion you've just told us about?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
