utterances.text: Were there any references to Dubrovnik in those materials that you looked at?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: How many of those bulletins did you see while you were in Zagreb, roughly speaking?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Maybe three or four.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Those bulletins, do you remember if they contained references to other places, to clashes, to problems on the ground, or anything of that nature?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So after eight days in Zagreb, you leave for Belgrade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Where you stayed for two days. Can you tell us where precisely, who you contacted there, what you did there. What was your brief in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: A convoy of monitors left Sarajevo to go to Belgrade. After we were there, we waited to find out how many of the monitors would stay in Belgrade and how many would go on to Sarajevo. We were informed by the head of the monitor mission in Belgrade that some of us would be selected to move to Sarajevo where the mission was to be expanded. The day after I arrived in Belgrade, I was informed that I would be one of the monitors that would be sent to Sarajevo. Two days after we arrived in Belgrade, the convoy left, including myself, and we arrived into Sarajevo where we became part of the ECMM mission for the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who the head of mission was in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I cannot recall his name, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And who was the head in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: The head of the mission in Zagreb was the ambassador who was from Holland. His name was Dirk van Houten.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You found him when he came to Zagreb on the 1st of October?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I met with him during the period I was in Zagreb. I don't know what date it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When precisely, then, did you start your mission in Sarajevo? Do you remember the exact date?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date. It's notated in my diary, but I don't have my diary with me at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Why is it that you don't have your diary with you?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I have just taken up an appointment with the United Nations in New York. The diary was part of the shipment of my personal possessions that was on its way to New York. However, when I was called here to the Tribunal, my shipment had not arrived. I assume it's now in a box on the harbour of New York awaiting my return.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: How many times have you testified before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: This is the second occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In addition to giving direct evidence in the courtroom, did you give any statements, written statements? Did you make any written statements to anyone in relation to your testimony?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I made out a written statement in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When giving this statement, in view of the many events involved and the length of the period you spent in Bosnia on the mission, were you in a position to make this statement on the basis of your memory only, or did you have to refer to your notes?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: The basis of my statement in 1996 was based on my recollection, on my notes, on documentation which I possessed, and on my diaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you remember in which period in 1996 and where you gave this statement?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I gave the statement to the Tribunal here in The Hague. I recollect it was approximately June or July of 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And when giving this statement, as you said, you used your notes, your diary, and everything else that could help you jog your memory while being interviewed by the investigators. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to the investigators another time as well in relation to the matters mentioned in your statement?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I spoke with the Tribunal team in the year 2000 as well, and also in the year 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me more specifically when it was in 2000 that you talked to them.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly what month it was in the year 2000. I was back here in June, July of 2003, and I testified in August 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me in relation to the year 2000, do you remember who you talked to?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I can remember some of the people that I spoke with. I have them on record. I don't have the record with me to give exact details.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And what about 2003? Can you tell me who you talked to then.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I talked to the team that were involved in the case against Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know any names?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you give us some names, if you remember them.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: One of the names was Linda Patrick.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Anybody else?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I spoke with one of the Prosecutors. I can't recall her name. I spoke with other people during that period that I was here in 2003. I spoke with Susan Somers. I spoke with Richard Kaufman, amongst others.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you remember when you talked to Ms. Somers and Mr. Kaufman?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I spoke with them in August 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you remember at what time you talked to them?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, I can't remember exactly what time I talked to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you remember perhaps that that was around noon?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that it was about noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether it was in the morning?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I think it was in the late morning, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was that in August 2003?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you remember which part of the month of August it was?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: It was towards the end of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: During that talk, did you write a statement that had to do with the interview, the conversation that you had?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I don't understand. Would you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: After the talks you had with the Prosecution towards the end of August last year, 2003, as you said, did you write a statement? Did you sign a statement that embodied the content of the talks you had with them?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I signed a statement. I didn't write it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you read the statement that you signed?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you agree with its content?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, did you have your notes with you and the diary that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you hand any documents over to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you recall what it was that you handed over on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I handed over a photograph that was taken on the 6th of December in the company of General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you hand the original of this photograph over to the Office of the Prosecutor, and do they still have it?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, they don't have it. It was taken. It was copied. And it was returned to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, did you write anything down on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: On that occasion, I wrote on the photograph the names of the people who appeared in the photograph and signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You said that you wrote the names of the people and that you signed that. If I understood you correctly, you did that on the back of the photograph. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: My understanding was that what I written on the back of the photograph was that which I had written after I had met with General Strugar. I'm not too sure whether it was on the same photograph or it was on a similar -- on a document that I articulated the names of the people who were in the photograph. That was done not in 1991, but in the year 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Who took this photograph on the 6th of December 1991?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: The photograph was taken by my interpreter, Darko Ivic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what kind of camera Darko Ivic had?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. It was my camera. It was a Minolta.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I assume that this is an ordinary camera that would be loaded with film, and then this film is developed and then photographs are made. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: After the 6th of December, did you have any other important meetings in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I had important meetings in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the time I became chief to the time I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Am I right if I say that you had everyday activities in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina that involved a great deal of travel on your part in order to organise meetings and to have meetings held in the area?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: A lot of my meetings were held in Sarajevo. But on occasions, I would travel to meet people that I wished to meet. So yes, there was a certain amount of travel. But it wasn't every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you have your picture taken with anybody else during that period?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: With your own camera?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who it was.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I had a photograph taken with many people. Sometimes with my own camera, with my own camera specifically I had a photograph taken with the chairman of the international peace conference Lord Peter Carrington; with Lord Carrington's representative who came to Bosnia, who was a Portuguese diplomat, Jose Cutileiro. I had photographs taken with some other military people of the JNA Army, specifically General Jankovic, and I had photographs taken on other occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what your motive was to have your picture taken with all these people?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I was interested in keeping a historical record of my service in former Yugoslavia as head of the monitor mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: During the many meetings that you had, I believe, with the top representatives of the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina during that period, did you keep any notes? Did you take any notes?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I would first of all put an entry into my diary as to who I met on these occasions. And on occasions, I would submit a report on the content of these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And did you write anything in your diary except for the names of persons you were meeting with, time, and place involved, or this particular information pertaining to these persons?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, it was of a very general nature. I would put down the name of the person that I met, the date that I met them, and maybe one or two comments. But other than that, no. Some reports I made out were separate, and they would have gone directly to the headquarters of the monitor mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did these meetings, did some of them perhaps last longer? Did some of them involve the resolving of particular issues? Were they actually negotiations?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Most of the meetings were over a prolonged period of time. And yes, on occasions, they involved negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: At these meetings, or rather, after a particular meeting with one side, would you have a meeting with the other side and then convey the response of the first side to the other side, and then in turn of the second side to the first side?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: All of the meetings I had with the generals of the federal army and of those that were considerable were all one side. It was a courtesy visit to the commanders of the JNA units throughout the entire republic. All of those meetings were generally one sided where I would meet out of courtesy the commanding officer. I would speak with him, and after those meetings, I wouldn't meet with anybody else. The other meetings that were nonmilitary, it was my practice to meet all sides. Therefore, if I went to a particular opstina, I would meet with, for example, the leaders of the Serb party. I would then meet with the Croats. And then I would meet with the Muslims. It was the practice to meet all sides. So in answer to your question, yes, I spoke with all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did the JNA have a problem with itself? What was the point of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: The point of the meetings was to make the mission known to the federal army because the first meeting I had with the first general who was General Kukanjac in Sarajevo, he admitted to me he knew very little about the monitor mission. So I decided that in order to explain to the senior military commanders of the federal army what we were about, I ought to go and visit them. And this is what I set out to do. And I met with the senior commanders in Trebinje, Bihac, Sarajevo, Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In view of your mission, once you would make these commanders aware of what your mission was, did you receive any requests from the JNA and its representatives?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I don't remember any specific requests, but I certainly remember some of the issues that I brought up with the commanders. Most of these were criticisms from the non-Serb communities who had certain criticisms of the actions of the federal army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did the federal army ever complain to you of paramilitary formations, of attacks against their members; that is to say, JNA members, JNA facilities, JNA vehicles? Did they ask for any intervention in that respect?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Some of the issues that were raised by the federal army would be of that nature, that yes, that paramilitaries from one side or the other were interfering in their movement. Some of these issues that were brought up by the JNA leadership were counter to some of the issues that I had raised with them. For example, that the JNA were arming a lot of the Serb communities. They weren't arming the other communities. That some of the JNA were interfering in the issue of the requirement for conscription or for the call-up, that the JNA were not assisting in the Croat and Muslim communities. And I was aware when I was head of the monitor mission in Bosnia that it was the view of the presidency that they looked upon the presence of the JNA as what they termed "an army of occupation." It was I, as head of the monitor mission, that persuaded the presidency to open up dialogue with the federal army. So over the period of six months, there were many issues that were brought up by me to be addressed by the JNA and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: At these meetings, did the JNA representatives provide you with any information that they had in relation to the activities aimed against the JNA?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I don't understand by what you mean by the word "any information."

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Well, for example, did any of the commanders say to you "I'm responsible for such and such a zone, such and such units are under my command; attacks were launched against the members of my particular unit at a particular place at a particular time" and so on and so forth? Did you receive this kind of information from them?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I never received any information from any JNA commander as to the extent of his zone of operation, nor did I seek it. I certainly would have received reports from JNA commanders that a person or persons were carrying out attacks from time to time. This is what they alleged. I had no proof of this. I think we have to understand that the time I was in Bosnia, there was a conflict going on. So it is inevitable that there would be reports to and fro of various attacks or interference in the JNA. But it was not part of the monitor mission to attempt to ascertain any military information from a JNA formation as to the content of his troops or his area of operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Since you said that the Bosnian authorities treated the JNA as an occupation force and that you considerably contributed to persuading the Bosnian authorities to talk to them, was it your impression at the time that these two sides were in conflict at that time?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I was generally aware as head of the mission of a concern being expressed by the presidency that the agreement that had been reached in which the JNA were to withdraw from the territory of Croatia would result in a considerable buildup of JNA forces on the territory of Bosnia. And the presidency at the time were concerned that a certain percentage of the JNA Army that was coming into Bosnia would turn itself into a Bosnian Serb army. And these were some of the concerns that were being expressed to me by the Bosnian leadership at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In October, November, and December 1991, you were with the mission in Bosnia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Throughout that period of time in the territory of Bosnia Herzegovina, were there any attacks that were launched against JNA members or features throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, there were no major attacks during that period of time conducted against the JNA in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you know about the presence of Croatian paramilitary units in Bosnia at the time and the attacks that they carried out against JNA units and facilities?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I personally did not know of the presence of Croatian paramilitary units in Bosnia. But I do know that there were allegations from the JNA that these activities were taking place. So I had no evidence either to lead me to believe it was happening or not. I did suspect that there was a considerable Croatian paramilitary influence in Western Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you try to verify it all, that -- the claims that you received from members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I would. I would have asked the teams, the monitor teams, who were in -- who were deployed in those areas to give me reports which would either back-up the claims of the JNA or disagree with the claims of the JNA. On some occasions, it was agreed that there was a considerable activity down in the area of Western Herzegovina by paramilitaries against the JNA. And I would have been satisfied with the reports of the monitor teams that there were occasions when attacks were leveled against the JNA forces, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Those attacks were launched by whom?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: We assume that the attacks were being levelled against the JNA by paramilitary forces. Exactly who they were or where they came from, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Neum is?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Which republic is that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: It's in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was it in Neum that you came across something interesting that was related to the subject of my questions?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. I was conscious that when I visited Neum that there was a considerable Croatian influence in the location. I was aware that the Croatian flag was being flown considerably. I was also informed that the Croatian currency was being used considerably. And I was sufficiently concerned about this to make it the subject of a report which I submitted both to my own headquarters in Zagreb and to the presidency of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you observe any paramilitary units from the Republic of Croatia or their presence in Neum?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, I did not observe any paramilitary units from the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of December, when you talked to General Strugar, did you know what his position was specifically?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I knew General Strugar to be the senior JNA military commander in the area that I visited, which included Trebinje and Bileca. I did not know the extent of his area of operations. And I did not know whether that area of operations included any of the territory of Croatia. As I previously mentioned, it was not in the nature of our mission to ascertain any detailed knowledge of military units.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On the day you visited him, was General Strugar the commander of a battalion, or perhaps of a brigade, or perhaps a different position?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I knew that General Strugar was a lieutenant general, and I know that lieutenant generals are commanders of major, large units such as corps, divisions, or combinations of both which would be the same as an operational group. I was satisfied that General Strugar was the highest-ranking JNA general in that location. And therefore, I had sought a meeting with him on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What unit was that, the military unit that he led? What was the name of that military unit?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I understood the military unit to be the 2nd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us more specifically in your understanding what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: My understanding of that would have been he would have been a three-star general, and that he would have maybe one or two generals under his command who would have commanded a unit within that operational group.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You'd call this unit an operational group. Is this something that you arrived at yourself, or did someone actually tell you that that was the name of the unit?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I was told by the monitors who were based in Mostar that this was an operational group.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did they tell you which operational group specifically? The 3rd, the 5th, the 27th perhaps?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I understood from recollection that it was the 2nd Operational Group. That's as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if you were told this before you met General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I don't recall. I was simply satisfied that General Strugar was the senior JNA commander of that entire area. And that was sufficient for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: A while ago, you said that when you talked to him, he was still lieutenant general in terms of rank. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: That was my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please specify "that was my assumption." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: It means that it was my belief he was a lieutenant general.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of December, was he actually lieutenant general or not?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: It was my assumption that on the 6th of December he was a lieutenant general.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you distinguish between the various General-level ranks in the JNA at the time?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I would have been able to distinguish between the various General-level ranks because on most occasions they would have been introduced to me as a one-star general, a two-star general, or a three-star general. As I said, it was my understanding that General Strugar was a three-star general. And in my army, a three-star general is called a lieutenant general, and I understand that to be the case in many armies.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you did not see any stars attached to General Strugar's uniform? Someone came and told you that he was a three-star general. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, then, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Can I please have the usher's assistance. I would like to show the witness Exhibit P47. This is the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Doyle, can you please tell us who is in this photograph and point the individuals out to us, from left to right, please.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: The person on the left-hand side of the photograph is the senior operations officer of the ECMM mission for Bosnia, Mr. Dermot Coogan. The person on the right-hand side of the photograph is myself, Colonel Colm Doyle, at the time head of the ECMM mission for the Republic of Bosnia. And in the centre is the officer commanding the 2nd Operational Group, General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What sort of uniform was General Strugar wearing? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: He was wearing the uniform of the federal army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please try to describe it more closely, what did it look like?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: It was a green, DPM uniform, with appropriate markings of the Yugoslav National Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What sort of markings? Where were those markings exactly?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: My understanding is the markings would either have been on the sleeve or on the front of the uniform. I can't remember exactly. And the rank marking would normally be held on the cap which, of course, he wasn't wearing on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Would the rank be displayed anywhere else save for the cap? Did you see the marking of a rank anywhere with the exception of the cap?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see the cap because he wasn't wearing one. So that doesn't apply. As far as I know, the rank -- to the best of my recollection, the rank would have been on the front of the tunic but I can't be certain of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You said that the uniform was DPM and that it was a JNA uniform. Was there anything else about the uniform that struck you as exceptional or characteristic?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This photo that you handed over to the Prosecution, is it originally a colour photograph?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And the only thing you remember is that the uniform was green?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: It was DPM, which is disruptive-pattern green.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you say so, then?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I did mention that it was DPM, which stands for disruptive pattern.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, this handwriting under the photograph, you said that you wrote that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can just please have the photograph back on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This spot where General Strugar's name is mentioned, can you please read out how exactly the line continues. What are these remaining words and what do they mean?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Are you referring to the second line of the notation?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: The first word is G-E-N for general; the second word S-T-R-U-G-A-R. After that there is O-C. Next there's the figure 2. That's followed by a capital O and a small p, and that's followed by a capital G, followed by a P and a full stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What you just read out to us, can you please expand and tell us exactly what it means.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: First word GEN stands for general. Second word is the General's name. The O-C stands for officer commanding. The number 2 stands for the number of the unit, which is the second. The Op stands for operational, and the GP stands for group. In other words, General Strugar, officer commanding the 2nd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So, you wrote this down during the talk that you had in August 2003 last year, the one you've referred to when you talked to members of the OTP. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So you did have this photograph as you were being interviewed by the OTP, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please now turn the other page of the document. And read out the first line of the text that follows.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: First line reads: With, w-i-t-h, the OC, that O-C, followed by the figure 2, followed by the word "corps," c-o-r-p-s, and followed by the word group, g-r-o-u-p.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This O/C, does that also stand for commander?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Officer commanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And what does the 2nd Corps mean?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I wrote on the back of that photograph believing at that time that General Strugar was officer commanding the 2nd Corps Group. It was corrected later by the monitor mission team and they told me it should have been the 2nd Operational Group. I wrote from the back of that photograph when it had been developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So what we've just been reading is what you wrote on the back of the photograph in -- from 1991. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If this relates to General Strugar, then you wrote down that he was the commander of the 2nd Corps in the group.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: That's the formation I told -- I was told he commanded at that time. I later found out it was incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I assume that you are well able to distinguish between corps and operational group, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So what we see on page 1, what you wrote down on page 1, which was the first thing that we read, where you say that General Strugar is the commander of the operational group, this is something you added after you were told by the OTP what his position was. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, this is something that I knew before the OTP told me. I was aware that it was an operational group that he commanded. At the time I visited him, I wasn't too sure. All I knew was that he was the senior JNA military commander in the area. Whether that was a corps or a group or an operational group, I wasn't too sure. So where the title of the unit that he commanded was a corps or an operational group, for me it didn't make a huge amount of difference because it didn't make any change to the fact that General Strugar was the commander or was the senior JNA commander of whatever military formation was in that area. I originally thought and I'd been told it was a corps group. It was then corrected afterwards that it was an operational group. And therefore, when I was asked to notate on the photograph was copied here, I had written down the corrected formation that I knew he had commanded, which at that stage I knew to have been the 2nd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me when exactly was it that you found out that he was, in fact, the commander of the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I would have been aware that the officer commanding the 2nd Operational Group by the time the formal visit was made in February of 1992 by Ambassador Salgueiro, who was head of the monitor mission. But I cannot be too sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let us try to be a little more specific. A year after the meeting, you were, for example, certain that he was the commander of the operational group.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. I was certain that he was the commander. I was certain that he was the senior JNA commander of that operational area. Regardless of whether it was a corps group or an operational group, I was satisfied that he was the senior JNA commander in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Doyle, you are a soldier, a professional soldier. There is no such thing as corps group, as you should know, whereas operational groups are very common. I do believe you are well aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. I only know the formations in relation to my own army. And at the time I went to Bosnia, I wasn't too sure what the military formations were at the highest level because the military formations in Yugoslavia were exceedingly far greater than those that existed in the Irish Army, which is quite small.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you know what the components were of the operational group at the time?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: My understanding was that if you had an operational group, that that operational group would consist of more than one corps. There could have been two corps. That would have been my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you know which corps belonged to this specific operational group?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I can't recall them offhand, but they were written down in our -- in the ECMM files which we had. So I assumed that there would have been at least two corps that would made up an operational group.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know where those corps were stationed?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: My understanding is that the corps were stationed in the Trebinje/Bileca area. I don't know how far it extended because as I mentioned before, it was not the nature of the monitor mission to look for detailed military information on any formations or units.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: As far as the operational group is concerned, when you learned that General Strugar was the commander of the operational group, did you say so when you gave your first statement to the investigators of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I don't recall. All I know is that I would have -- as part of my witness statement, I would have mentioned that General Strugar was the senior -- most senior JNA military commander in the area. I don't know whether -- I made my statement, whether it said it was corps group or whether it was operational group. To me, that was just a technical point. The main point that I would have made in my witness statement was that on the 6th of December, I met with the most senior JNA military commander of the area. Whether that was a corps or an operational group to me was immaterial. He was the senior military commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you again: When you talked to the investigators of the OTP for the first time, were you actually aware of the fact that General Strugar was the commander of the operational group?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure that in 1996 I would have put down in my witness statement that he was the commander of the corps group or the operational group. I can only repeat that I was satisfied that when I made my statement it was in the knowledge that General Strugar was the senior JNA federal military commander in the area in question. Of that, I had no doubt.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. It's not in the nature of an objection, but if I can if we will be finishing with cross today as the Prosecution's case was put in 46 minutes, and I think we're into about an hour and a half if I'm not wrong on cross. If I can just get some guidance as to whether I would be able to get into redirect today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't believe that I will be able to conclude my cross-examination today given what this witness stated during the examination-in-chief. He is a material witness to our case, and I will have plenty of questions to ask him in connection to his credibility and the credibility of his testimony before this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your answer surprises me very much, Mr. Rodic. I thought that you had covered the quite limited area of the evidence quite well already. But you must carry on for the moment. I hope you will be able to finish by the end of today.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Doyle, can you tell me about the remaining part of your note, annotation. What is it?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Do you wish me to read the notation?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: There's no need for that. I do have a translation here, and we all have the English original. Can you just tell us what it mean, what it stands for, the remainder of it.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: What it means is that General Strugar admitted to me through his interpreter that he had launched an attack on Dubrovnik, an artillery attack on Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The note is unfinished. What else is there?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: The last two words read: "Killing 16."

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Where did you get this bit of information?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did General Strugar tell you himself?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I do not believe that he did, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are these casualties?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it true that this was a later addition?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: The notation on the back of the photograph would not have been done any earlier than when the photograph was developed. When that was, I simply don't know, but I am satisfied it would have been within a relatively short period of the meeting with General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you give us an approximate time frame as to when the photographs were developed?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I would say within two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So unless General Strugar himself told you, gave you this piece of information related to the 16 people who had been killed, how else did you come by that piece of information?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I do not recall. I might have read it in a report. I simply cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can I have the usher's assistance, please, to show the witness Exhibit P46, which is an extract from the witness's diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: For the record, can you please read back to us the second passage of your note that refers to the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: The numbers there are 1200. That indicates time. Met with General Strugar (three star) followed by the words "bad in Dubrovnik." Underneath that is the notation "back to Mostar." And finally underneath that is O-N, which stands for overnight, which meant I stayed overnight in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Your strongest impression from your meeting with General Strugar, in addition to general information concerning the time of the meeting and his rank, is what you added "bad in Dubrovnik." What precisely is that supposed to mean?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: What it meant in the diary was that Dubrovnik suffered on that occasion, and that's why I wrote the words "bad in Dubrovnik."

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You provided exceptionally detailed information during your testimony today in answer to a question by the OTP. Would it not have been natural for you to write down what struck you as particularly bad in Dubrovnik or as early as the 6th of December, which is when you spoke to General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, it would not, because it was not in my practice to put detailed notes in my diary. The practice for my diary was simply to note who I met and where I met. So it is not unusual that I had no notation other than that on that particular Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: How come, then, that as early as 12.00 you knew for sure that it was bad in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Because I didn't write in the diary at 12.00 on that day. I wrote in the diary that evening. Or in fact, I probably wrote in that diary when I returned to Sarajevo. So the notation in the diary are after the events took place, rather than a reminder of the events that were to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Your answer strikes me as logical. It seems very convincing to me that probably you added that upon your return to Sarajevo. Once in Sarajevo, did you follow coverage of the situation on TV?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps recall whether you watched any TV coverage on the situation in Dubrovnik related to the 6th of December 1991 specifically?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, that may well have been the case. I simply don't recall now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it perhaps possible that after watching that coverage, you added the sentence about the situation in Dubrovnik being bad? Because after all, you say yourself that this was a later addition after your return to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was it -- was there anything else that you did on that day that was important?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: After finishing my meeting with General Strugar, I had a meeting with the mayor of Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was your most important objective upon your arrival in Trebinje to meet with General Strugar or with the mayor?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: The objective of my visit to Trebinje was specifically to meet with General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was it an established part of your work, the work of your mission in Bosnia to meet with mayors and presidents of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Why, then, is there no note in your diary of that? No note of your meeting with the mayor of Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Because there was no pre-planned itinerary to visit the mayor of Trebinje. It came as an afterthought that while I was there, maybe I should meet the mayor. I do not recall who suggested it. It may well have been General Strugar. I simply do not know. But I did meet the mayor of Trebinje for a very short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You add these notes later, you say. So why did you not enter this, too, in your diary?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Because to me, the meeting with the mayor of Trebinje was only secondary to the meeting with General Strugar. The meeting with General Strugar was officially set up in advance. The meeting with the mayor of Trebinje was not. The diary that I made out covered the main events. It did not necessarily cover every single meeting I had with everybody for six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct if I say that you organised your meeting with General Strugar primarily with the objective of meeting him in the first place?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct if I said that you did not have any specific task in respect of General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In fact, it is correct that was the first you ever met that man. Right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: During the examination today, you often used the word "impression," what your impressions were. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about information, then? What was conveyed to you, was it actually scant so then you had to infer things on the basis of your own perception and observations during these meetings?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I'm not sure I can understand that question. Would you repeat it for me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you infer things on the basis of your impressions because information was scant? There was not enough information presented at that meeting or meetings?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I think it is normal at a meeting when you meet people that you obviously have an impression of that person or those persons. I think that's natural. And this was no different from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: It is correct that you did not have any notes kept at the meeting or after the meeting with General Strugar. Right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that what you said here that you received by way of information from General Strugar was the result of what the lieutenant colonel who was interpreting told you?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: All of the information that was given to me at that meeting came through the interpreter, who I would presume was correctly translating what the general was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What was his English like? Can you remember that? Can you remember what kind of English he spoke?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: The lieutenant colonel who interpreted spoke English to a very high standard and had been used consistently by the leadership of JNA units in that capacity as an interpreter/translator. So his standard was very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What is the name of this lieutenant colonel?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I do not have the name of the lieutenant colonel on record. I certainly have him on videotape and on some of the meetings that we had which were recorded by the mission, his name. But I don't have his name to hand at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you have an interpreter at the meeting? Did you have an interpreter who had come along with you?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Who was your interpreter?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: His name was Mr. Darko Ivic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did he spend a lot of time working with you?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was he only an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: He was more than an interpreter in that he facilitated the setting up of meetings on behalf of the presidency of Bosnia. So he acted as liaison to the mission from the presidency. He acted as my interpreter. And he acted on my behalf when I requested the setting up of meetings with various groups and personalities in the mission area. He was one of two interpreters supplied by the presidency of Bosnia to assist the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Darko Ivic is a member of the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware. I know that he was supplied as official liaison to the monitor mission. My understanding, he was a police lawyer, but we never discussed matters of that nature. He was there purely to act on requests that I made and to act as my interpreter when that was required.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you have this kind of a liaison officer, to put it that way, from some other side who was also a member of your team?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Would you explain when you say "some other side." I don't understand what you have in mind there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If Darko Ivic was a liaison officer on behalf of the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, then he represents that side, vis-a-vis your mission, and he organises meetings for you, of course, availing himself of the position of the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that side that he represented. I'm just asking you whether from some other side, from the JNA or anywhere else, you had this kind of a liaison officer who was with you all the time attending meetings and so on?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: No, when I was head of the mission, the interpreters we used were both interpreters made available to us from the presidency. I should point out at this meeting with General Strugar, the only person who interpreted was the JNA commander. At no stage of the meeting with General Strugar was there any translation or interpretation done by Mr. Ivic. It was all done by the JNA, and that was a courtesy I extended to the JNA because General Strugar's office was facilitating me, and I felt it courteous to allow the exchange of comments that were made by General Strugar to me to be interpreted by the JNA interpreter and not Mr. Ivic. So Mr. Ivic did not have any part in that meeting. He didn't speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was Darko Ivic present in the room where you held the meeting?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you go to Sokolac once with Darko Ivic?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I believe I did. I can't remember exactly. I went to so many places in Bosnia with him that I can't recall all of them. But we properly would have passed through that location on one of the visits I would have made to or from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Sokolac is?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: My understanding is it is in the general vicinity, not too far from Mostar. Somewhere between Mostar, south towards Trebinje. But its exact location, I'm not too clear on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me why after the meeting that was held with General Strugar took place you did not inform the mission about it? Why did you not file a report about the meeting?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: The reason I didn't file a report was for two reasons: One, because I was newly into the appointment, and this was more or less a courtesy visit I was making to the teams and to the JNA commanders. That was the first reason. The second reason was that there was a mission already in place in Croatia. It was deployed there by the headquarters in Zagreb, and that location would have included places like Split and Dubrovnik. It was my assumption that if any action had been seen to have taken place in the area of Dubrovnik, it would have been reported on by the mission inside Croatia. My terms of reference were strictly confined to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And they are the two reasons why I didn't make a specific report. Also, I should say that that trip that I made was over a period of three days, and I met -- I had maybe five or six meetings, including the meeting with General Strugar. So the meeting with General Strugar was just one of a number of meetings I had during that trip. So I did not make any detailed report of those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did your mission have its headquarters in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: The headquarters of the entire monitor mission which covered all of the republics of former Yugoslavia was located in Zagreb, Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Isn't that unusual when you say that you did not write a report because it was your first time, because you were a new person there in view of your experience in various theatres of war until then that you've already referred to?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I've given the reasons why I didn't write the report. If I was to rewrite the book again, I possibly felt that I should have. But at the time, I didn't make the report. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The principle of work was to file reports. Isn't that right? You were in Bosnia, but your mission was also operating in Croatia. So if you learned of important information in Bosnia that was relevant to Croatia, wasn't that all supposed to go to headquarters where all reporting would be channelled to? Wouldn't that be logical?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, it probably would be logical. But as I said, I was newly into the appointment. It was my first visit outside of Sarajevo. And I choose not to make a report for no other reason than it was my first visit. It was a number of visits -- or meetings that I had in the area. And as I said before, any activity that would have occurred down in the area of Dubrovnik, I would have expected to have reported by the mission that was in Croatia. So in hindsight, it would have been better had I submitted a report; but in reality, I didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In view of your impression from that meeting and when answering the Prosecutor's questions, you said that you experienced something that you had never experienced before that in your military career. I'm asking you once again, and also bearing in mind what you wrote on the back of the photograph concerning the number of casualties and this confirmation of shelling, doesn't this bear enough weight as it was? Would you not want to report about that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: The fact is I didn't report it, and I cannot change that now. If I was to do it again, it would have been better had I made that report. But I can't change what didn't happen or what did happen. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you tell the Prosecution that General Strugar was commander of the 4th military district?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I'm not too sure. I can't remember what I told them except that I did tell them that he was the senior JNA military commander in that entire area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that during your first interview with the Prosecution investigators, you did not mention the operative group and General Strugar at all, or rather that you did not say that he was commander of the operations group. You said that he was commander of the military district, the 4th Military District. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I don't have my witness statement in front of me, so I can't recall exactly. It was a considerable statement. But if it's written in the statement, as you say it's in the statement, then that's what I said. I have no argument with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Aren't you being contradictory then in relation to the answers that you gave here today in terms of your knowledge that General Strugar was commander of the operations group? And you said that you certainly became aware of that within a year after the meeting. And then there is the time when you gave your statement to the investigators of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: That may well have been the case. I'm not too sure. It wasn't an issue at the time when I went out the witness statement [sic]. I do know that when I spoke with the Prosecutors in 2003, I was certainly aware at that stage as to what the formation of this operational group was. I had no particularly -- occasion at which I had to dwell on the events which took in place in 1991, 1992. I've done many things since that time. And I am satisfied now, having seen documentation, that General Strugar, in fact, commanded the 2nd Operational Group. But I want to repeat that at the time I made a statement in 1996, it was to convey to the investigators that General Strugar was the senior JNA military commander of the major formation that was in the area of Trebinje and Bileca. Whatever that formation was called, in my view, is secondary to the fact that I could identify him as the senior JNA military commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I have the statement that you gave to the investigators. The statement was given, at least according to what it says here, in 1995 rather than 1996, which is what you said here. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, if it was 1995 and it's signed, then I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 34 of your statement, you say, and I am going to read it out to you: "On that same day, before I met with the mayor" --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. The statement that we have is not numbered by paragraph. If you could ask that we have a page number it would be more helpful. Perhaps putting it to the witness we'll see if that would be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, I take it this isn't your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, regrettably, it's not. Because I have to draw some comparisons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. If that's the case, I think we've gone past the time for today. You might collect the information that Ms. Somers needs when we resume tomorrow. I'm afraid I must ask you to return tomorrow, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We resume at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 4th day of February, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
